A black stone similar to a bean is found in the Nile, and when it is seen, dogs do not bark; you shall carry a dog’s tongue kept under your thumb in your shoe, or if you carry a dog’s dried heart with you, from Sextus; hare’s hair, or dung, from Pliny. Or you shall carry a young weasel’s severed tail in your foot, or you shall give it a frog in a morsel, all these things are for avoiding the barking of dogs. Nigidius says that dogs flee the sight of him all day who expels a tick from a dog and has worn it for some time. Oppianus:

> *But if you carry a small piece of a hyena’s skin*
> *Removed at once, both the whelps and fierce dogs*
> *Struck by harsh terror, will not bark at you thereafter*
> *As you approach, even if they had barked before.*

### *So that a dog cannot run.*

If you smear the wings with oil, for it will be hindered in running, in this way it will happen.

### *So that a hawk may be spirited.*

You will animate a bird against its prey, so that it may attack large birds; steep the food which it uses during the time of hunting in wine, or if it is a goshawk, give a little vinegar; when you wish for it to fly, give it three morsels of meat steeped in wine, or pour wine into the mouth of a pigeon chick, then make it fly. Thus

### *You will make partridges more pugnacious,*

If you give them sprigs of maidenhair fern <note>original: "adianti"</note> in their food, from Pliny, and

### *Roosters become more pugnacious,*

By giving them garlic in their food when they are about to fight; from which, most wittily in an old comedy, they are called <term>ἐσκοροδισμένοι</term> <gloss>garlic-fed</gloss>, that is, garlic-fed in place of a vehement person, and one too prone to battle.

### *So that a bird may not fly on high,*

Pluck the feathers of the tail that direct the course upwards, thus it will fly in a circle below. If you wish

### *That a bird cannot fly,*

Cut the upper and lower nerves of the wing, and it remains without harm; the bird will not fly, and in this way they do not flee in aviaries.

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>is made bright through piety, religion, prudence, <note>the Latin *prudentia* here denotes wisdom or discernment</note> and the worship and veneration of God, as if truth were perceived by the eyes of reason. By the confidence of this faith, he stands out among men just as the sun surpasses the other stars with its light. The sun itself illuminates the other stars not so much by the magnitude of its divinity as by its holiness. Believe, O Asclepius, that this sun is a second god, governing all things and illuminating all living beings in the world, whether they are animate or inanimate. For if the world is a living creature <term>animal mundus</term> <gloss>the world as a living entity</gloss> that has always lived, and exists, and will exist, there is nothing mortal in the world. For in every living part that exists within the world, just as in one and the same living creature that always lives, there is no place for mortality. Therefore, God himself must be most full of life and eternity, if it is necessary for him always to live. The sun, therefore, is like the eternal world, and thus it is the governor of vital things, or the frequent visitor and dispenser of all their vitality. God is, therefore, the eternal governor of the living or vital things that are in the world, and the eternal dispenser of life itself. He has dispensed this once by an eternal law, providing life to all vital beings in the manner I shall describe.

<summary>This passage describes the sun as a secondary god and the eternal governor of all living things within the world. It asserts that because the world is a living and eternal entity, it contains no true mortality, with God acting as the ultimate source and dispenser of life.</summary>
<keywords>Sun, Asclepius, divinity, living world, eternity, governance, life, vitality</keywords>

Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro, a Roman scholar.</note> testifies that he saw these things. And there are even more marvelous things than these: for on the Attic shore, the sea sounds like a lyre. In Megara, a certain rock produces the sound of a stringed instrument when struck, so great is the power of Music. It soothes the soul itself, lifts up the mind, incites warriors to battle, and relieves the labors and fatigue of individual tasks. It calls back those who have fallen and despaired, and comforts travelers. The Arabs say that camels carrying burdens are comforted by their leaders who sing to them. In a similar way, those bearing heavy loads sing, and they are strengthened and lightened by it: for song produces pleasure and dexterity, it mitigates the irascible, gladdens the sad and anxious, pacifies the discordant, and dispels vain thoughts. Hence it is that Democritus and Theophrastus affirm that some diseases of the body and mind can be cured or inflicted in this way. Thus we read that Terpander and Arion of Methymna <note>legendary Greek musicians known for their skill with the lyre.</note>

For the good is innate to truth, together with life and light, and no avenger came to pass beyond it. Truly, all the avenging powers were cast back by a certain sudden impulse. You have understood, my son, the mode of rebirth itself. The intellectual generation is composed by the present number of ten <term>denarius</term> <gloss>the number ten</gloss>, which rejects the number twelve <term>duodenarius</term> <gloss>the number twelve</gloss>. And we have contemplated this from the generation itself. Therefore, whoever, because of the kindness of the generation which is according to God, loses bodily sense, knows himself to be composed of divine things and, having become unswerving, rejoices in the divine power with his whole mind.

**TATIUS.** O father, I conceive this not by the intuition of the eyes, but by the act of the mind, which is exercised through the inner powers. I am in heaven, in earth, in water, in air. I am in animals, in trees, in the body, before the body, and after the body. But I would have you tell me this further: how are the avenging shadows repelled by the ten powers? What is the method, Trismegistus?

**TRIS.** This tabernacle, O son, is constituted from the zodiacal circle, which consists of that number twelve. And the numbers are eleven, plus one, all-formed according to the ideas of nature, for the wandering of man and his circuit. Therefore, those avenging powers are in a way separated from one another, yet in acting they are in a way joined. As for example, recklessness is inseparable from wrath. Rightly, therefore, according to right reason, they are distant only insofar as they are repelled by the ten powers, that is, by the number ten. The number ten, O son, is the generator of the soul. But life...

<summary>Hermes explains to Tatius how the intellectual generation of the soul, governed by the number ten, rejects the twelve zodiacal powers of the physical world and how these avenging forces interact in the human experience.</summary>
<keywords>regeneration, rebirth, denarius, duodenarius, zodiac, intellectual generation, avenging powers, divine power</keywords>

Therefore, the gods are the princes of all species; these are followed by those gods whose prince is <term>ousia</term> <gloss>essence/substance</gloss>. These are sensible, of both origins and similar to each other, who accomplish all things through sensible nature. Each one illuminates its own work through another. The heaven, or whatever is understood by that name, is <term>ousiarches</term> <gloss>ruler of essence</gloss>, Jupiter. For through heaven, Jupiter provides life to all things. The <term>ousiarches</term> of the sun is light. For the good of light is infused into us through the orb of the sun. Of the thirty-six stars fixed forever in the same place (whose name is Horoscopii), their <term>ousiarches</term> or prince is he whom they call <term>Pantomorphon</term> <gloss>all-formed</gloss> or Omniform. He, through diverse species, makes diverse forms. The seven spheres which are called erratic have their <term>ousiarchas</term>, that is, their princes, which they call fortune, <term>eimarmenēs</term> <gloss>fate/destiny</gloss>, by which all things are changed, with the law of nature, most firm stability, and varied by eternal agitation. Truly, the air is the organ, or machine of all things, through which all things are made. There is, however, a second <term>ousiarches</term> of this, for mortals are mortal, and things like them. Therefore, with these things being so, moving from the lowest to the highest, all things pertaining to themselves are naturally connected to one another, so that to mortals, mortal things and sensible things are joined to sensible things; but the height of governance obeys that highest lord, so that they are not many, or rather are one. For all things depend on one, and from it they rather flow down; when they are distant, they are believed to be many, divided. But when unified, they are one or rather two, from which all things are made and by which they are made. That is, from the matter from which they are made, and from His will, by whose nod other things are effected. ASCLEPIUS: This again is the reason, O Trismegistus. TRISMEGISTUS: Such it is, O Asclepius. For God, whether as father or lord...

For indeed, arsenic can by no means be fixed, unless the artist operator has an equal knowledge of its tingeing spirit, regarding which all philosophers have slumbered, attempting in vain to effect anything from it. Whosoever, therefore, is ignorant of this spirit, let him have no hope of fixing it, nor of attributing to it the virtue by which it might acquire the perfection of transmutation. For this reason, I make it known to all that the whitening about which mention has been made is derived from a false foundation, and that by it copper is falsely whitened, not transmuted. Sophists, having disguised and painted Venus <note>the alchemical name for copper</note> in this manner, mixed it with double its weight of lunar <note>the moon/silver</note>, and sold it to goldsmiths and moneyers; but finally, they transformed themselves into counterfeiters, not only those who sold it, but also those who bought it. Some of the sophists, in place of white, took red arsenic, and this too went into a false art. For in whatever way it may be prepared, it exhibits nothing but whiteness. Some have gone further, to common sulfur, which they cooked in vinegar, lye, or very sharp urines for a day and a night, until it emerged white. Afterward, they elevated it from common salt and eggshell by sublimation, and cooked and sublimated it, and that many times; nevertheless, it remained always combustible, though white: yet, to fix raw mercury with it...

<summary>The author warns against fraudulent alchemical practices, specifically the attempt to use arsenic or common sulfur to "whiten" copper, which results in mere surface deception rather than true transmutation.</summary>
<keywords>arsenic, Sophists, whitening, Venus, copper, sulfur, transmutation, counterfeiting, sublimation</keywords>

where they should have taken <term>pyrite</term>, <term>sulfur</term>, <term>salt</term>, <term>metal</term>, and various other materials, they took substances in which there is no operation; and although these things are expensive in shops, they have no value at all in the work. Our material is not bought from any shop, yet it is found there daily, and merchants throw it into the streets. It is sufficient, therefore, that it be found for free. But the material of our <term>stone</term> is compared to all those things with which the craftsmen work. For our stone is our <term>salt</term>, our <term>mercury</term>, <term>verdigris</term>, <term>saltpeter</term>, <term>sal ammoniac</term>, <term>Mars</term> <gloss>iron</gloss>, <term>sulfur</term>, and infinite other things of this kind, yet not dug from wild fields or mountains with hammers and other tools. But our stone is extracted solely from our own mountains and fountains: in our <term>salt-fountain</term> our <term>salt</term> is found; from our earth our metal, <term>mercury</term>, and <term>sulfur</term> are poured, and not from wild, foreign, or field mountains, which the craftsmen do not understand, nor can they believe or comprehend. For the Lord has obscured and stopped their senses, for which reason they used these things otherwise than they ought to have been used, and they did not aim at the target at all. Nevertheless, they persisted in this contrary sense and complied with their own stubborn heads; for when they should have <term>distilled</term> <gloss>extracted essence via heat and condensation</gloss> gently, they <term>sublimed</term> <gloss>vaporized and condensed into solid form</gloss> with a strong fire; they scorched the <term>aqua fortis</term> <gloss>strong water/nitric acid</gloss>, and immediately burned the operation of nature and the substance itself, reducing it to nothing. When they should have <term>dissolved</term>, they <term>coagulated</term> instead; and again, like those unskilled in things, they handled the matter unskillfully and fell into doubt, claiming with lying words that the art is not true but false, in which they themselves rightly lie. For their own ignorance shamefully deceived them, which must be imputed to their own obscure and dark cunning, when, according to their own obscure intellect, they interpreted words otherwise than they sounded. For example, when the Philosophers spoke of <term>calcining</term> <gloss>reducing to powder</gloss> (which they call grinding), those unskilled <term>philosophasters</term> <gloss>fake philosophers</gloss> understood it as burning, and reduced the substances entirely to ashes, so that nothing could be made from them. When the Philosophers <term>dissolve</term> or transmute into water, those <term>nosy ones</term> <gloss>arrogant meddlers</gloss> burned the nature with <term>aqua fortis</term>, and the same water, which has no [power] in

Likewise, lest it happen that one err in <term>Jupiter</term> <gloss>Tin</gloss>, on account of the difficulty of its reduction, so that if at any time one places its lime into reduction, it happens to him that it does not reduce, but finds it in its prior disposition or turned into glass, and judges its reduction impossible. For we say that if one does not apply a great fire in the reduction of <term>Jupiter</term>, it will not reduce. If, indeed, one applies a great fire, it does not necessarily happen that it reduces, but it is possible that it reduces it into vitrification <note>the process of turning into glass</note>. And that is because <term>Jupiter</term> has in the depth of its nature a fugitive substance of <term>argentum vivum</term> <gloss>quicksilver/mercury</gloss> enclosed. Which, if it draws out a long delay in the fire, will flee, and will leave the body deprived of humidity, so that it is found more apt to be converted to vitrification than to the fusion of a metallic body. For everything deprived of its own humidity gives no fusion other than vitrifying. And therefore it is necessarily left that, with the most rapid force of fire, one hastens to reduce it quickly. For otherwise it is not reduced. Therefore let him practice at that, and he shall know. 

The <gloss>second</gloss> mode of calcination of these two bodies, <gloss>Saturn and Jupiter</gloss>, which is perfected by the acuteness of salt, is that a quantity of salt be thrown upon their face, quantity after quantity most often in their fusion, and mixed by much agitation through an iron rod, over the fire, until they are turned into ash through the mixture of salt. And afterward, let their lime be perfected through the same mode of perfection, with its considerations. But in this there is also a difference in the calcination of these two bodies. Because <term>lead</term> <gloss>Saturn</gloss> is converted into powder more easily from the first labors of calcination than <term>Jupiter</term> <gloss>Tin</gloss>, yet its lime is not perfected more easily than that of <term>Jupiter</term>. The cause of this depends on the fact that <term>Saturn</term> <gloss>Lead</gloss> has a more fixed humidity than <term>Jupiter</term>.

829. Since religion resides in the highest parts of a person, and from those highest parts their lower parts live and shine, and because Mohammed occupies their minds together with their religion, therefore some Mohammed is always placed in their view. And so that they may turn their faces toward the East, upon which the Lord is, he is placed below the Christian center. It is not the Mohammed himself who wrote the <term>Alcoranum</term> <gloss>Koran</gloss>, but another who performs his duty; nor is it always the same person, but he is changed. Once it was a man from Saxony who, captured by the Algerians, became a Mohammedan; because he had also been a Christian, he was at times moved to speak with them about the Lord, that He was not the Son of Joseph, but the Son of God Himself. Other Mohammeds have succeeded this one later. In the place where that representative Mohammed has his seat, a fire appears like a torch, so that he may be known; but that fire is not visible to others than Mohammedans.

830. The Mohammed himself, who wrote the <term>Alcoranum</term>, does not come into view today. I was told that in the earliest times he presided over them, but because he wished to rule over all things of their religion as God, he was cast out from his seat, which he had under the Papists, and sent down to the right side near the south. Once, a certain society of Mohammedans was stirred up by malicious people to acknowledge Mohammed as God. In order that the sedition might be quelled, Mohammed was brought up from the lower earth and shown, and then he was also seen by me. He appeared like those bodily spirits who have no interior perception, his face inclining toward black, and I heard him speaking these words: *I am your Mohammed*; and soon he seemed to subside.

831. The Mohammedans are hostile to Christians primarily because of the belief in three Divine Persons, and from that, the worship of three Gods and just as many Creators; and furthermore to the Roman Catholics because of their genuflections before images, and hence they call the latter idolaters and the former fanatics. They say that they make a three-headed God, and that they say "one" but mutter "three," and therefore that they rend Omnipotence and make three out of one; and that they are like fauns <note>mythological creatures often depicted with horns</note> with three horns, one for each god, and together three for one, and that thus they pray, thus they chant, and thus they sound from the pulpits.

832. The Mohammedans, like all nations that acknowledge one God and love what is just and do what is good from religion, have their own Heaven, but it is outside the Christian one. However, the Mohammedan Heaven is divided into two. In the lower one, they live honestly with several wives, but from there, no others are elevated into the higher Heaven except those who renounce their concubines, and acknowledge the Lord our Savior, and at the same time His dominion over Heaven and Hell. I have heard that it is impossible for them to think that God the Father and our Lord are one, but that it is possible for them to believe that He rules over the Heavens and Hells because He is the Son of God the Father. This faith among them is the means by which ascent into the higher Heaven is granted to them by the Lord.

833. That the Mohammedan religion has been received by more kingdoms than the Christian religion can be a stumbling block to those who think about Divine Providence and at the same time believe that no one can be saved unless they were born a Christian. But the Mohammedan religion is no stumbling block to those who believe that all things are of Divine Providence; these inquire in what this lies, and they also find it. It lies in this: that the Mohammedan religion acknowledges the Lord as the Greatest Prophet, the Wisest of all, and also as the Son of God. But because they have made the <term>Alcoranum</term> the only book of their religion, and hence Mohammed, who wrote it, has settled in their thoughts, and they pursue him with some worship, they therefore think little of our Lord. In order that it may be fully known that this religion was raised up by the Divine Providence of the Lord to abolish the idolatries of many nations, it will be told in some order, but first concerning the origin of idolatries. ### On the images of the Head and Tail of the Moon's Dragon. Cap. XLV.

<note>A woodcut depicts a serpent coiled into a circle resembling the Greek letter Theta (Θ). The creature has the head of a hawk and a pointed tail. Within the circular body, there is a central vertical line crossed by a shorter horizontal line, with small symbolic marks at the terminals.</note>

They also used to make an image of the Head and the Tail of the Moon's Dragon <note>the lunar nodes, the points where the Moon's orbit intersects the ecliptic</note>, namely, the figure of a serpent between an airy and a fiery circle, with the head of a hawk surrounding them in the likeness of the Greek letter theta. They made it when Jupiter held the midheaven with that head. They affirm that this image contributes much to the success of petitions. They wished to signify by this image a good and happy <term>daemon</term> <gloss>spirit</gloss>; they desired to represent him through the image of a serpent, for the Egyptians and Phoenicians celebrated it as a divine animal above all others, and celebrated its divine nature because in it, above other animals, there exists a sharper and more ample spirit or fire. This is shown both by its swift movement without any feet, hands, or other instruments, and because it repeatedly renews and rejuvenates its age.

Truly, they made the image of the Tail similarly, when the Moon was eclipsed in the tail, or was badly affected by Saturn or Mars. They made it to induce anxiety and infirmity, and they called it an evil spirit. A certain Hebrew had enclosed such an image in a golden, double belt, which Blancha, the daughter of the Duke of Bourbon, gave as a gift to her husband Peter, King of the Spains, the first of that name (whether knowingly or unknowingly). When he was girded with it, he seemed to himself to be surrounded by a serpent. Having subsequently discovered the magic power inserted into the belt, he repudiated his wife for that reason.

### On the images of the Mansions of the Moon. Cap. XLVI.

They also used to make images in the individual <term>mansions of the Moon</term> <gloss>the twenty-eight segments of the lunar path across the zodiac</gloss>. The premise stating that the will is what specifies one of two identicals is correct, but the premise stating that the world is in a vacuum that surrounds it is false, or at least not self-evident. Furthermore, there follows from his postulation of this vacuum an abhorrent consequence for them, which is that it would have to be eternal; for if it were created in time, it would require a vacuum. As for the premise stating that nothing can come from the will except a created thing, that is not self-evident. The reason is that the will which is in act exists along with the act of the thing willed itself, for the will is among the relative terms <note>original: *min al-muḍāf*, a reference to the Aristotelian category of relation</note>. It has been clarified that when one of two relative terms exists in act, the other exists in act, like father and son; and when one of them exists in potentiality, the other exists in potentiality. If the will that is in act is created, then the thing willed is necessarily created in act; and if the will that is in act is eternal, then the thing willed that is in act is eternal. As for the will that precedes the thing willed, that is the will which is in potentiality—meaning that whose object has not yet passed into actuality, since the act necessitating the creation of the thing willed has not been joined to that will. Therefore, it is clear that when its object has passed into actuality, it is in a state of existence in which it was not before the passing of its object into actuality, since it was the cause of the occurrence of the thing willed through the mediation of the act. Thus, if the theologians <note>original: *al-mutakallimūn*, scholars of *kalām* or speculative theology</note> were to posit that the will is created, it would necessarily follow that the thing willed is created, and this is unavoidable. The outward meaning of the Revealed Law <note>original: *al-shar‘*, religious law</note> does not delve into this depth with the common people; therefore, it does not explicitly state that the will is either eternal or created. # A Chapter on the Distinction of Their Sects, Their Religions, Their Signs, Their Stations, and Their Tales

Before this, in the mention of <term>Abū al-Ḥasan Nūrī</term>—may God have mercy upon him—I had said that they consist of twelve groups. Two of them are rejected, and ten are accepted. Each of these classes possesses a good practice and a praiseworthy path in spiritual struggle <term>mujāhadāt</term> <gloss>disciplined exertion</gloss>, and a subtle etiquette in spiritual vision <term>mushāhadāt</term> <gloss>contemplations of the Divine</gloss>. Even though they differ in their practices, spiritual struggles, visions, and ascetic exercises <term>riyāḍāt</term> <gloss>self-discipline</gloss>, they are in agreement and consensus regarding the foundations and branches of the Law and the declaration of Divine Unity <term>tawḥīd</term> <gloss>monotheism</gloss>. <term>Abū Yazīd</term>—may God be pleased with him—said, "The disagreement of the scholars is a mercy, except in the abstraction of Divine Unity." This well-known report is in agreement with this.

The truth of Sufism <term>taṣawwuf</term> <gloss>mysticism</gloss> exists among the reports of the sheikhs in terms of reality, and is divided in terms of metaphor and convention. Therefore, I shall, by way of brevity and conciseness, speak to explain those divisions, and I shall spread a carpet for each one in the foundation of their path, so that the seeker may obtain knowledge of it, so that for the scholars it may be a weapon, for the disciples a rectitude, and for the lovers a salvation.

The passage that acknowledges <term>YHWH</term> <gloss>The Tetragrammaton, representing mercy</gloss> and <term>Elohim</term> <gloss>God, representing judgment</gloss> signifies that they are enacted through all the qualities that are completed by the attribute of judgment and the attribute of mercy. Just as you find in the creation of the first man, in his judgment, in his expulsion, and in all those matters, you will find that they all came about through the attribute of judgment and the attribute of mercy, and everything is in complete perfection through mercy and judgment, everything according to what is fitting in true judgment.

According to this principle, the Torah says: "The Rock, His work is perfect" <note>Deuteronomy 32:4</note>. The interpretation of the verse is as follows: The Rock who decrees judgment with strength does not act in cruelty. He does not decree judgment unless His work is perfect, meaning the judgment He decreed was first deliberated between the two attributes, loving-kindness and judgment. This is the meaning of "His work is perfect." For the word "perfect" <term>tamim</term> contains the secret of two things. It is as if it said "twins," except that in honorable language, he said "perfect" regarding the two things from above, and below he used the word "twins." Thus it is said: "And they shall be twins below, they shall be perfect together at its head" <note>Exodus 26:24</note>. Below, they are twins; above, they are perfect. Because below, they appear as two things, a thing and its opposite, as one helping and one accusing, but above, everything is one intention. Whether helping or accusing, both have one intention, and there is no hatred or love there, no partiality, but only true judgment. Therefore, he said "His work is perfect," for He deliberated in judgment and mercy and decreed the judgment; this is the secret of true judgment.

Regarding that which is said, "For all His ways are judgment," this means everything is for the eye of every observer, as it is said, "For all His ways are judgment." You already know that judgment is included in judgment <term>din</term> and mercy <term>rachamim</term>. For judgment corresponds to Jacob, who is the middle line, the one who mediates between the two tents, which are Abraham and Isaac. Abraham corresponds to loving-kindness, Isaac to judgment, and Jacob balances between them, "a plain man, dwelling in tents" <note>Genesis 25:27</note>. Judgment corresponds to Jacob, drawing from loving-kindness on the side of Abraham and from judgment on the side of Isaac. Thus it says: "Judgment and righteousness in Jacob You have made" <note>Psalm 99:4</note>. The prophet said: "Correct me, YHWH, but with judgment, not in Your anger, lest You bring me to nothing" <note>Jeremiah 10:24</note>. The interpretation of the verse: "Correct me, YHWH, but with judgment." What is said "but" <term>ach</term> is a division, meaning half the attribute of judgment, which is loving-kindness. For judgment is half judgment and half loving-kindness. Therefore, he said "but with judgment," and said afterwards, "not in Your anger, lest You bring me to nothing," revealing the secret to diminish half the judgment on the side of anger. Therefore, judgment depends on Jacob, who is our father among the tribes. He knew the great sorrow of the children when the Holy One, blessed be He, decrees judgment upon them, that he should seek mercy and righteousness for them. The secret is: "And YHWH of Hosts shall be exalted in judgment" <note>Isaiah 5:16</note>. What is written after it? "But the Holy God is sanctified in righteousness." This means that when YHWH of Hosts is exalted in judgment, it leaves behind judgment and makes room for the attribute of **El** <gloss>God</gloss>, which is the secret of what was said: "And the Holy God is sanctified in righteousness." In sum, when YHWH of Hosts is exalted in judgment, the attribute of **El** comes, which is from above, and performs righteousness, and judgment is performed. This is the secret of what they said: judgment is included in loving-kindness and judgment. And it says: "Judgment and righteousness in Jacob You have made." The great secret is: "Righteousness and judgment are the foundation of Your throne" <note>Psalm 89:15</note>. For righteousness is sometimes judgment according to its reception of the flow, as explained, for righteousness is great judgment in strength. But when judgment is shared with it, then the throne is established in mercy. And if it is exalted in judgment and reaches until loving-kindness and truth together, they are called the shining faces, then everything is made into great mercy. ### On the shame felt from undeserved praise.
## D I A L. XXVI.

> Praise sparingly, for when you praise unworthily,
> If you condemn later, it will be a mark of fickleness.

*Sorrow.* I am accused of having praised an unworthy man.

<note>A large ornamental letter L marks the beginning of Reason's response.</note>

*Reason.* You are accused of having praised an unworthy man. An evil deed, indeed, often arises from a good root. For good and innocent men—such as they themselves are—judge others to be the same. Hence, they are even more prone to praise than they should be; and although I admit that to praise an unworthy person is a mistake, it is still much worse to disparage one who is undeserving.

*Sorrow.* I have praised an unworthy man.

*Reason.* If you did so knowingly, you are reprehensible; but if unknowingly, you are excusable. It is a lesser evil to be deceived than to deceive. To be deceived is the misfortune of another, but to deceive is the crime of the deceiver himself.

*Sorrow.* The praise of another is turning into my own infamy.

*Reason.* Rather, it is your own fault or ignorance. For from the praise of another, just as from their blame, there is no real infamy for you.

*Sorrow.* I grieve deeply that I have praised an unworthy man.

*Reason.* See to it, then, that you do not grieve over this same thing often. Take care not to leap rashly into praising or blaming. <meta>continues from previous page: ...as they contain other things, and the one being purged must not hasten to take much or poor-quality food, lest nature draw it in without it being digested. If anything of that sort is required, it must be done little by little, spaced out until it is gradual, and what enters the body must be well-digested. Bloodletting is the specific form of evacuation for a balanced state <note>in terms of blood volume</note>. As for evacuation specific to an excess of a humor in quantity or its corruption in quality, that is other than bloodletting. Every evacuation that is excessive causes fainting in most cases. Whoever induces the cessation of diarrhea that has become habitual <note>must be careful</note>, for the ailment of returning that evacuation to its habitual state is something that causes it to grow in most cases, such as one who causes the cessation of a nosebleed; for if one restores it, it removes the blockage. Know that the remaining part of the material that needs to be evacuated is less receptive to investigation and being brought to the point where strength fails, and nature often resolves that remainder. As long as the humor is of the appropriate type and the patient can bear it, do not fear excess. Sometimes you may need to purge until fainting occurs. Whoever has strong constitution and a large amount of corrupt humors, purge him little by little, and likewise if the material is highly mature or strongly mixed with blood, such that it cannot be purged all at once. This is the case with sciatica, chronic joint pain, cancer, chronic scabies, and chronic boils. Know that diarrhea draws from above and clears from below, so it is consistent with the standard attraction, and it is also consistent after the materials have settled. If the materials are from below, they are drawn to it by contradiction, and it clears them from where they are by the act of attraction, and vice versa. The status of bloodletting varies according to the locations from which the blood is taken, as you have learned. The people least in need of evacuation are those with good digestion, and inhabitants of hot climates have little need for evacuation.

We say that it is recommended for one who wishes to induce diarrhea to separate or divide their food, and the first amount he tries in a day <note>is to be done</note> in intervals, and to make them different foods and different drinks. For the stomach is susceptible in this state to longing to push what is in it upward or downward. As for food that is not different, but rather relying on other food, the stomach becomes full with it and becomes sluggish, clutching it tightly, especially if it is small in quantity. As for one who is naturally loose-bowelled, nothing of that sort is needed. Know that the need for vomiting, diarrhea, and the like does not occur for one who has good regimen; he needs what is lighter than that. It may suffice for him to be concerned with exercise, rubbing, and cupping. Then, if his body becomes filled with the greatest level of the best humors, I mean blood, then bloodletting is what is needed for purification rather than diarrhea. If necessity dictates bloodletting or evacuation, such as in the autumn, and <unclear>one is to induce</unclear> vomiting, it is farther from bloodletting. This is from the precepts of Hippocrates and the books of his followers, and it is the truth. Likewise, if phlegmatic humors are mixed with blood, and if the humors are balanced, viscous, and cold, bloodletting might increase their thickness and viscosity, so it is necessary to begin with diarrhea. In sum, if the humors are balanced, give precedence to bloodletting. If an evacuation prevails after that, and if they are not balanced, evacuate the superfluity first until it becomes balanced, then bleed. Whoever gives the medicine before bloodletting should have given bloodletting a few days prior. Whoever was recently bled and needed an evacuation, drinking the medicine would have stopped it, and often drinking the required medicine while bloodletting is occurring causes fainting and distress. If it is not calmed by sedatives, then bloodletting should have preceded it. Not every evacuation is needed for excess fullness, as the magnitude of the ailment and the fullness according to quality and quantity dictate it. Often, good regimen takes the place of bloodletting when required at the time, and often the necessity calls for evacuation but an obstacle arises, so there is no strategy for it except fasting, sleep, and correcting the imbalance in the way of fullness. Among the evacuations, there is that which is for the sake of precaution, such as what is needed for one accustomed to gout, epilepsy, or other such things at a known time, especially in the spring, so he needs to take precautions before its time and perform the evacuation specific to it, whether it be bloodletting or diarrhea. Sometimes the use of desiccants from the outside and drying medicines is a form of evacuation, like what is done for those with dropsy. Sometimes you are forced to use a medicine that is similar in quality to the humor being evacuated, like colocynth when you need to evacuate bile, so it is necessary to mix with it what is contrary to it in quality and similar to it in diarrhea, like myrobalan. Addressing an imbalance if it occurs later in patients with inflammation of the viscera, it weakens their diarrhea. If you are forced to do that, use for them things like ivy and safflower. As for the purgative and cassia, that is what Hippocrates said: "Whoever has a stomach that is easily responsive to vomiting, the first thing in his purification is to use vomiting in the summer or spring when the time is right, for that clears the body of fatigue." Know that the one who drinks it is accustomed to loose bowels, or is not accustomed to vomiting in the summer and avoids it when not needed. It is necessary to decide before diarrhea, which is by refining the humor that one wishes to evacuate and widening the passages at that time, for that clears the body of fatigue. Know that the one who drinks it is accustomed to loose bowels or is not accustomed to vomiting before using the strong medicine, from one of the regimens <note>of</note> thinning and diarrhea, and diarrhea with emaciation of the abdomen is difficult and tiring and mixes, and the vomiting medicine might return as a purgative if the stomach is strong, or if it is drunk under intense hunger, or if the drinker is accustomed to loose bowels, or due to the medicine, or if the medicine is heavier in essence than in speed of descent. The purgative might cause distress due to weakness of the stomach or intense heaviness, or due to the medicine irritating it, or because its subject has indigestion. Every purgative medicine, if it does not purge the immature <note>humor</note>, it stirs the humor it is meant to purge and spreads it in the body, so it dominates the body and calls other humors to it, and that humor increases in the body. Among the humors, there is that which is more responsive to vomiting in most cases, like yellow bile. Among them is that which is resistant to vomiting, like black bile. Among them is that which has a state, like milk and stars <note>obscure: perhaps a reference to celestial timing or specific herbal combinations</note>, its diarrhea is more correct in itself. Whoever has his humor descending, such as those with slippage of the intestines, the intestines clutch and the purgative medicine fails. What is composed of medicines that are strongly different in the time of diarrhea, they disturb the diarrhea, and the first purges the second before the second purges, and perhaps the first purges the second itself. Whoever is exposed to diarrhea and his body is not purified by it, must have pain, colic, and distress affecting him, and what is evacuated is evacuated with great difficulty. In sum, the medicine that does not evacuate the superfluities does not have distress with it; when it is taken with distress, it either evacuates that which is not a superfluity, or if the evacuated humor changes from vomiting or diarrhea to another humor, it indicates the purification of the body from the humor intended to be evacuated.

And You are holy, enthroned upon the praises of Israel. And one called to the other and said: "Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of Hosts; the whole earth is full of His glory." Then a spirit lifted me, and I heard behind me a great and mighty sound, blessing and saying: "Blessed be the glory of the Lord from His place." Then a spirit lifted me, and I heard behind me a sound of great quaking, of those who praise and say: "Blessed is the glory of the Lord from the place of His dwelling." The Lord is King for ever and ever. The Lord's kingdom endures for ever and ever. O Lord, God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, our ancestors, keep this forever for the impulse of the thoughts of the heart of Your people, and direct their heart to You. And He, being merciful, forgives iniquity and does not destroy; He frequently turns back His anger and does not stir up all His fury. For You, O Lord, are good and forgiving, and abundant in loving-kindness to all who call upon You. Your righteousness is righteousness forever, and Your Torah is truth. Grant truth to Jacob, loving-kindness to Abraham, as You swore to our ancestors from days of old. Blessed is the Lord day by day; He bears our burden, the God of our salvation, Selah. The Lord of Hosts is with us, a stronghold for us, the God of Jacob, Selah. O Lord of Hosts, happy is the person who trusts in You. O Lord, save; the King will answer us on the day we call. Blessed is He, our God, who created us for His glory and separated us from those who go astray, and gave us a Torah of truth, and planted eternal life within us. May He open our hearts to His Torah and place in our hearts His love and His awe, and to do His will and to serve Him with a whole heart, so that we may not labor in vain nor be born for chaos. May it be Your will, O Lord our God and God of our ancestors, that we keep Your statutes in this world, and that we merit and live and see and inherit goodness and blessing for the years of the Messianic era and for the life of the world to come. So that my glory may sing to You and not be silent; O Lord my God, I will thank You forever. Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord, and the Lord shall be his trust. Trust in the Lord for ever and ever, for in God the Lord is a Rock of ages. And those who know Your name will trust in You, for You have not forsaken those who seek You, O Lord. The Lord desired, for the sake of His righteousness, to make the Torah great and glorious.

O Lord, our Lord, how majestic is Your name in all the earth.
Be strong and let your heart take courage, all you who wait for the Lord.

A prayer of David: Incline Your ear, O Lord, answer me, for I am poor and needy. Preserve my soul, for I am pious; O my God, save Your servant who trusts in You. House of Jacob, come, and let us walk in the light of the Lord. For all the nations will walk, each in the name of its god, but we will walk in the name of the Lord our God for ever and ever.

To incline our hearts to Him, to walk in all His ways, and to keep His commandments, His statutes, and His ordinances, which He commanded our ancestors. But if the soul knows that something is truly so, and if it is not possible that the thing be otherwise, then the soul cannot be deceived. But how then does God foreknow these uncertain future events? For if He deems that things are avoidable which cannot possibly come to pass, He is deceived, which is impious to believe or even to suggest. But if He discerns that things are to be in such a way that He knows them either as possible to happen or possible not to happen, what kind of foreknowledge is this that grasps nothing certain or stable? Or how is this any different from that famous prophecy of Tiresias <note>A blind prophet from Greek mythology</note> who said, "Whatever I say will either be or not be"? Why then should divine prudence differ from human opinion if, like men, He judges things to be uncertain when their outcome is uncertain? But if, in that most certain fountain of all things, there is nothing uncertain...</meta>

<summary>This passage explores the philosophical paradox of divine foreknowledge, questioning how God can possess certain knowledge of future events if those events are not themselves necessary.</summary>

Third article: whether the more universal things are prior in our intellectual cognition.

It is proceeded thus, to the third. That the more universal things are not prior in our intellectual cognition: because those things that are prior by nature are posterior and less known to us, but universals are prior by nature of our intellect. Furthermore, composite things are prior with respect to us than simple things, but universals are prior <note>original: "cioza" (likely a scribal error for *simpliciora* or *simplicia*)</note>: they are known later with respect to us. Furthermore, the philosopher says in the first book of the <term>Physics</term> that the defined falls into our cognition prior to the parts of the definition, and the parts are less universal: just as "animal" is a part of the definition of "human," and universals are known later with respect to us. Furthermore, effects we encounter both by chance and by principle, but universals are known later with respect to us. But if it is what [the Philosopher] says in the first book of the <term>Physics</term>, [we must proceed] from books into singulars to arrive [at knowledge]. I answer that it must be said that in the cognition of our intellect, two things must be considered. First, that intellectual cognition in some way takes its beginning from sensitive [cognition]. And because the sense is of singulars, and the intellect is of universals, it is necessary that the cognition of singulars with respect to us be prior to the cognition of universals. Second, it must be considered that our intellect proceeds from potency to act. And that which proceeds from potency to act arrives first at an incomplete act, which is between potency and act, and a perfect act. The perfect act to which the intellect arrives is complete science <note>original: "scia" (abbreviation for *scientia*)</note> through which things are known distinctly and determinately; the incomplete act is imperfect science through which things are known indistinctly under a certain confusion. For that which is known in this way is both known in act and in a certain way in potency, as he says in the first book of the <term>Physics</term>: the things manifest and certain to us are more confused. Afterward, however, we know by distinguishing the principles and elements. It is manifest, however, that to know something in which many things are contained without having the proper knowledge of each one of those things contained within it is to know something under a certain confusion. In this way, however, both a whole in which parts are contained in potency and an integral whole can be known: for both wholes can be known in a certain confusion without the parts being known distinctly. However, to know distinctly that which is contained in the whole, or to have cognition of a less common thing: just as to know "animal" indistinctly, and to know an animal in which there is rational or irrational, which is to know a human or a lion. Therefore, it occurs to our intellect first to know "animal" and to know "human." And if I compare any [notion] to [another] as greater or lesser, just as the sense exits from potency into act, so does the intellect; that order...

<column-break/>

of cognition appears in the sense. For [the object] is more in the sense, and I distinguish more; and when it is known less, it is more remote through <unclear>that which pertains to being a body</unclear>, and what pertains to being an animal, and more pertains to being an animal and what pertains to being a substance; and first [a substance] and so on. Or it pleases, and it is evident that a child from the beginning distinguishes [a human] from [an animal]; and children from the beginning call all men "fathers." Afterward, however, he terminates each one, as [the Philosopher] says in the first book of the <term>Physics</term>: for [it is] manifest that he who knows something indistinctly still and in potency, he knows and [it is a fiction] and a principle, and thus he knows the species and he can: so that he knows the things [in it]. And thus, by itself, indistinct cognition is between potency and act. And that the cognition of singulars is prior with respect to us, and the cognition of the universal is [prior to] sensitive cognition and intellectual cognition. If [we consider] both sense and with the intellect, the cognition [of the singular] is more and is prior to the cognition of the lesser and the common. To the first, it must be said that through a double [way] it can be considered. One way is through the intention of truth. And since the intention of truth and truth are the same, it has a relation to many things. [So] it arrives, and the abstraction of the intellect is the end of this mode while truth is posterior. In the first book of <term>De Anima</term>, the universal either is nothing or is posterior: but [some] placed universals as substances <note>original: "suba"</note>, and in this consideration it is true: more so because particulars are not except through participation in the subsisting universals which are called <term>ideae</term> <gloss>Ideas</gloss>. In another way, it can be considered with respect to the nature itself of animality or humanity, as it is found in particulars. And thus there is a double order of nature. One according to the way of generation and time, when those things that are imperfect and in potency are prior. And in this way the [universal] is prior, and it is in nature, for that which appears manifestly in the generation of a human and an animal. For first the animal is generated, then the human, as [the Philosopher] says in the book <term>De Generatione Animalium</term> <gloss>On the Generation of Animals</gloss>. The other is the order of perfection or the intention of nature, just as act is simply prior to potency in nature, for that which is perfect is prior to that which is being perfected; and in this way the less universal is prior in nature, for a human is an animal. Nature in its intention does not stop at the generation of an animal, but it intends to generate a human. To the second, the more universal is compared to the less universal as a whole, and through the whole it becomes more universal, not only [regarding] a human and a horse, but as it can [contain] the less universal, it includes not only the [more universal] but also others, as "human" is not only "animal" but rational. Thus, therefore, "animal" considered in itself is prior in our cognition to "human," if "human" is prior in our cognition and "animal" is [known] through its reason. To the third it must be said that something can be known in two ways. In one way, absolutely, according to what it is in itself, and thus nothing [is known] of the house. In another way, when it is the parts of this whole, and the stones; it is necessary that we know the whole before the parts. For we know the house first in a certain confused way. Thus, therefore, it must be said that the defining [term] considered absolutely is prior to the defined. Otherwise, the defined would not be made known through those things. But rather they are the parts.

<summary>This text investigates the priority of universal versus singular cognition in the human intellect, concluding that while singulars are prior in the order of sensory generation and experience, the universal structure represents the ultimate intention of nature's perfection.</summary>

When the Lion woke the next morning, the judge entered to see him, accompanied by a group of the prominent members of his court, with the document containing what Dimna had offered as his excuses. The Lion took the document and ordered them to depart from him.

Then he sent for his mother and read the document to her. She was distressed by it and said, "If I speak harshly to you, O King, do not be angry."

The Lion said, "I will not be angry, so say whatever you wish."

She said, "I do not see that you know what harms you from what benefits you. I suspect that because Dimna has spent so much time manipulating you regarding his case, he will soon incite against you something you will not be able to stand up to or overcome."

She then stood and left in a state of anger. The next day, the judge sent for Dimna and brought him out. He consulted with the scholars regarding him, but they did not say anything.

The judge said to him, "Even if everyone present has remained silent and said nothing, their suspicions have gathered on the fact that you are a criminal. There is no good for you in life after your guilt has been settled in their hearts. I do not see anything better for you than to confess your crime. By doing so, you will free your neck from the burdens of the afterlife, and a good reputation regarding your case will return to you for two reasons: the first is your ability to find ways out and fabricate excuses <note>The text uses the word "Ma'adhir" meaning excuses or pretexts</note> that will defend you, and the second is your confession of your sin, choosing safety in the afterlife over safety in this world. For the scholars have said that death in a state of grace is better than life in a state of disgrace."

Dimna answered him and said, "Judges do not pass judgment based on their own suspicions, nor the suspicions of the common people, nor those of the elite. You know well that suspicion does not replace the truth in any way. Even if you have all suspected that I am the one who committed this crime, I have certain knowledge of myself, and my knowledge of myself is a certainty in which there is no doubt. My case has only become ugly in your eyes, if you are indeed so, because you have suspected that I strove..."

Confusion spread among all the king's people,
The hearts of the elite and commoners in the city were lost.
A powerful enemy is after us,
Or perhaps a disaster of the kingdom has risen from the Unseen.
Because the jester has struck, wild and coarse,
Having killed several Arabian horses on the road.
They gathered at the king's palace,
Why did such a rush and foolishness occur?
Due to his haste, the clamor of the mob increased,
Turbulence and anxiety gripped the city of Tirmidh.
One beats both hands on his forehead,
The other cries out from illusion and lamentation.
From the clamor, chaos, fear, and punishment,
Every heart fell into a hundred kinds of fancies.
Each person made a prediction based on conjecture,
Wondering what fire had fallen into the city.
He sought the path, and the king immediately gave way,
When he kissed the ground, he said: "Hey, what happened?"
Everyone who asked about the condition of that sour-faced one,
He placed his hand on his lips: "Hush!"
His illusion fuels this confusion of his,
Everyone became dumbfounded in his anxiety.
The jester signaled so that the King of Generosity,
Would let him speak for a moment.
So that reason might return to the ephemeral mind,
For I have fallen into a strange world.
After an hour, when the king, out of illusion and suspicion,
Had become bitter in both throat and mouth.
The jester had never been seen like this before,
For there was no companion more pleasant than he.
He always offered jests and wit,
He kept the king happy and laughing.
He would make him laugh so much in his assembly,
That he would grab his stomach and bind it.
That from the intensity of laughter, his body would perspire,
But today, he is so yellow and sour-faced.
Fell over laughing,
Suspicion upon suspicion and fancy upon fancy.
He put his hand to his lips: "O King, be quiet!"
Because the king's heart was full of grief and caution,
So that whatever punishment might come to the king.
He had killed many kings in that region,
For the Khwarazm-Shah was very bloodthirsty.
This sour king was in a state of suspicion,
Either through wrath or the power of that stubborn one.
He said: "Speak quickly, what is the situation?"
And by the jester's art, that illusion increased.
He said: "I heard in the village that the King,
Sent a crier to every royal road."
"That I want someone who will ride for three days,
To Samarkand and, if still..."
"I have offered riches and substitutes for him,"
"Since the goal is obtained from the message."
"I hurried toward it for that reason,"
"But I say I do not have that ability."
"Such baseness does not come from someone like me,"
"Do not spin this thread of hope upon me."

Frenzy became the state of all the madmen,
The peace of the elite and commoners of the city became agitation.
Either a powerful enemy has appeared,
Or some calamity of the kingdom has arrived from the Unseen.
The jester came in great haste, winding and twisting,
Why did he kill those Arabian horses on the road?
They gathered at the palace of the king of creation,
Why did he make such a display of speed, that jester?
With obscene language and useless haste,
There was a clamor and anxiety in Tirmidh.
The old man was beating his knees,
The other was wailing and tearing his hair.
Fear and turmoil changed the people,
Every heart fell into a hundred kinds of imaginings.
Everyone was making predictions based on thought and analogy,
They were saying, "What fire has fallen into the city?"
He sought the way and gave the way, as the King was present,
When he kissed the ground, he said: "What is this news, O King?"
Whoever asked about the state with much effort,
He would put his hand to his lips: "Be quiet, hush!"
Beyond what was appropriate, there was confusion and fancy,
They all became dumbfounded and speechless in their anxiety.
The jester gestured, "O King of Generosity,"
"Grant me permission to take a breath."
So that reason might return,
For I have fallen into a strange state.
After an hour, when the king was full of suspicion and doubt,
His throat and mouth became bitter and dry.
He had never seen the jester so tense,
For there was no one more cheerful and lively than him.
He was always playing with jokes and witticisms,
He kept the king happy and laughing.
He would make the king laugh so much,
That the king would double over holding his stomach.
His body would perspire from laughter,
He would fall over from his laughing.
He was counting him so sour-faced,
And with his hand on his lips, meaning "Hush!"
Illusion upon illusion, fancy upon fancy,
Would the king suffer some punishment?
The king's heart was full of grief and suspicion,
For the Khwarazm-Shah was very bloodthirsty.
He had destroyed many kings in that direction,
Either through tyranny or the power of that stubborn one.
The king was sour, troubled, and fearful,
And from the jester's performance, his anxiety increased.
He said: "I said in the village, O King,"
"Who is it that brings this noise, turmoil, and distress?"
"I want a man who will go in three days,"
"He has given orders without ambiguity."
"I would give him treasures in return,"
"That he should go to Samarkand and receive the gift."
"I hurried for that reason,"
"Since the purpose is achieved by the message."
"I have not the power,"
"For I say I do not have that capability."
"There is no strength in someone like me,"
"Do not pin this service on me."

The <term>Sufi</term> <gloss>mystic</gloss> sat by the wine jar in the corner of the monastery,
When he saw the <term>Muhtasib</term> <gloss>market inspector/censor</gloss> carrying a jug upon his shoulder.

I asked a wine-seller at dawn,
About the state of the <term>Sheikh</term> <gloss>elder/religious leader</gloss>, the judge, and the drinking of the Jews.

He said, "Though you are a confidant, the matter is not to be spoken of,
Restrain your tongue, keep the veil drawn, and drink wine."

O cupbearer, spring is arriving and there is no money left for wine,
Think of a solution, for the blood of my heart has come to a boil from grief.

Your love is poverty, youth, and the new spring,
Accept my excuse and cover my sin with the hem of your generosity.

How long will you use your tongue like a candle?
The butterfly of desire has arrived, O silent lover.

O King of form and essence, for one like you,
No eye has ever seen, nor has any ear ever heard.

Remain as long as your young fortune, from the ancient sky,
Allows you to wear the blue robe <note>original: "خرقه ازرق" - a symbol of asceticism often adopted by Sufis</note>.

Last night, a sharp-witted expert whispered to me,
"It is not right to hide the truth from the wine-seller."

He said, "Make things easy for yourself, for by its very nature,
The world treats those who struggle too hard with harshness."

Then he offered a cup whose radiance caused Venus in the heavens,
To start dancing and cover its ears as it played the lute.

Bring a smiling lip with a bleeding heart, just like the cup,
Do not cry out like a harp when a wound is inflicted upon you.

Until you become familiar, you will not hear the secrets behind this veil,
For the ear of the uninitiated is not the place for the message of <term>Soroush</term> <gloss>the angel of inspiration</gloss>.

### The Nahidiyya Maqama

Isa ibn Hisham narrated to us, saying:
I inclined with a group of my companions toward the courtyard of a tent, seeking hospitality from its people. A man came out to us, thin and lean. He said: Who are you? We said: Guests who have not tasted anything for three days. He said: Step aside. Then he said: O youths, here is a <term>nahidah</term> <gloss>a dish of curdled milk and herbs</gloss>, speckled like the head of a bald man, in a wide bowl, crowned with a piece of expertise from the regions of a giant, one of whose mouthfuls satisfies the hunger of a group of five, hungry with thirst, where the molar disappears. Its kernels are as if they were the tongues of birds. They season the <term>nahidah</term> in it with <unclear>coriander</unclear> that they have milked from the <unclear>aged, fat-rich</unclear> <term>jallad</term> <gloss>type of goat or livestock</gloss>. Do you desire it, O youths? We said: Yes, by God, we desire it. The old man laughed and said: And your uncle desires it too. Then he said: What is your opinion, O youths, of wheat flour white as pieces of bullion, sprinkled on a tablecloth with the scent of <term>qaraz</term> <gloss>acacia fruit</gloss>? A graceful, clever, light-hearted youth leaps to it, and kneads it without shaking or alarming it, then softens it into a fine, smooth dough. Then he flavors it with <term>sumac</term> or crushed spices in abundance. Then he intends to twist it and leaves it in a corner of the desert, until it has risen without cracking. He intends to find <term>ghada</term> <gloss>desert tree</gloss> wood and lights a fire in it. When the fire settles, he prepares his roasting space, then takes his dough and spreads it out after seasoning it perfectly. Then he spreads it over it, and covers it, and <unclear>smothers it with hot stones</unclear> until the two heats meet. When he covers them on the hot ashes with a lid, and it separates into layers, and its crust resembles companions, and its redness is like the redness of the Hijaz <term>busr</term> <gloss>ripened dates</gloss>, famous for [the] Mother of Rats or the cluster of Ibn Tab, he pours upon it white sauce like snow until it settles into the fats. The heart of the wheat flour drinks what is on it of the sauce. I present it to you, and you snatch it up in mouthfuls of <term>jawb</term> or <term>rankal</term> <gloss>types of bread</gloss>. Do you desire it, O youths? He said: Each of us yearned for his description, our saliva dripped, and we smacked our lips and clicked our tongues. We said: Yes, by God, we desire it. He said: The old man laughed and said: And your uncle, by God, does not dislike it. <meta>continues from previous page</meta>And when we saw ourselves worthy of setting down words that would endure after us, it became incumbent upon us that you should be the first to whom we present what we possess, and the first whom we acquaint with what we have learned. We would not have been right or just, nor would your pure mind have been served, had we cast before you the ultimate conclusions we reached before first establishing the principles with you. That would have provided you with nothing more than a matter of general tradition, provided you held a good opinion of us on account of our friendship and mutual understanding, rather than because we deserve that our word be accepted. We are not satisfied for you with anything higher than this rank, nor are we content for you with this lesser station, as it is insufficient for salvation, let alone for attaining the highest degrees.

We wish only to lead you along the paths we have already traveled, and to have you swim in the sea we have already crossed, until it brings you to where it brought us. You will then witness what we witnessed, and confirm through your own insight all that we have confirmed, thereby becoming independent of relying upon the knowledge we attained. This requires a certain, not insignificant amount of time, freedom from distractions, and a total dedication of your resolve to this art. If this determination is sincere in you, and your intention is truly prepared to engage in this pursuit, you will praise your journey when the morning comes, attain the blessing of your endeavor, and have pleased your Lord, even as He has pleased you. I am with you wherever you desire in your aspirations, and wherever your resolve and total focus may aim. I hope that I shall succeed in guiding you along the most direct path, and the one most protected from pitfalls and calamities. And if there is presented now to me a brief glimpse into

So you make the share one hundred and nine parts, and you multiply thirteen by one hundred and nine parts, and add to that eighty parts, which makes one thousand four hundred and ninety-seven, and the spouse's portion is three hundred and twenty-seven.

If you leave two sisters and a wife, and he bequeaths to a man the equivalent of a sister's portion minus an eighth of what remains of the wealth after the bequest, the method for this is that you establish the compulsory share <note>original: "farīḍa"</note> at twelve shares. Each sister has a third of what remains of the wealth after the bequest; thus, this is wealth minus a bequest. You know that an eighth of what remains with the bequest equals a sister's portion, so an eighth of what remains is an eighth of the wealth minus an eighth of the bequest. An eighth of the wealth minus an eighth of a bequest, plus a bequest, equals a sister's portion, which is an eighth of the wealth and seven-eighths of a bequest. The entire wealth equals three-eighths of the wealth and three bequests and five-eighths of a bequest. Subtract three-eighths from the wealth, and there remains five-eighths of the wealth, which equals three bequests and five-eighths of a bequest. The entire wealth equals five bequests and four-fifths of a bequest. The wealth is twenty-nine, the bequest is five, and the portion is eight.

Regarding another aspect of bequests: a man died and left four sons, and he bequeathed to a man the equivalent of one of his sons' portions, and to another a quarter of what remains of the third. Know that the bequest is only from a third.

3223. There are two lights by which man is illuminated: the light of the world and the light of heaven. The light of the world is from the sun; the light of heaven is from the Lord. The light of the world is for the natural or external man, and thus for the things that are within him. The things that are there, even though they do not appear to be of that light, nevertheless are; for nothing can be grasped by the natural man except through such things as exist and appear in the solar world, and thus unless they have some form derived from the light and shade there. All ideas of time and ideas of space, which in the natural man constitute so much that he cannot think without them, also belong to the light of the world. However, the light of heaven is for the spiritual or internal man. The interior mind of man, where his intellectual ideas—which are called immaterial—reside, is in that light. Man does not know this, even though he calls his intellect sight and ascribes light to it. The reason is that, as long as he is in worldly and bodily things, he has perception only of such things as belong to the light of the world, and not of those which belong to the light of heaven. The light of heaven is from the Lord alone; the universal heaven is in that light. This light—that is, the light of heaven—is immensely more perfect than the light of the world. Things which constitute one ray in the light of the world constitute myriads in the light of heaven. In the light of heaven there is intelligence and wisdom. That light is what flows into the light of the world which is in the external or natural man, and causes him to perceive the objects of things sensually. Unless that light flowed in, man would have no apperception at all, for the things that belong to the light of the world have their life from that source. Between these lights, or between those things which are in the light of heaven and in the light of the world, there is a correspondence when the external or natural man makes one with the internal or spiritual, that is, when the former serves the latter; and the things that then exist in the light of the world are representative of such things as are in the light of heaven.

Therefore, the Jewish method using temporal hours <note>unequal hours, determined by dividing the daylight period by twelve</note> does not function unless the conjunction for the beginning of the month of Tishrei coincides with the autumn equinox. It never coincides with it; rather, it often falls significantly before or after it, as we have clarified previously. 

Once we determine the time of the conjunction using the calculation provided by the Jews in the table which we analyzed according to their viewpoint, we proceed from that to knowing the beginning of the year and determining its status regarding deficiency, equilibrium, or fullness. We have already gained the knowledge of whether it is a simple or leap year. Thus, we look in the table of limits for a duration of weekdays whose boundaries contain the time at which the conjunction occurred for us: in the section for leap years if it is a leap year, and in the section for simple years if it is a simple year. Once found, we align it with the beginning of the week for that year and its status. When we know the beginning of the year and its status, and we combine that status with the simple or leap year designation, we then know from this the progression of the beginning of the following year.

This conclusion asserts that the Perfection of Wisdom itself should be meditated upon because it is Buddhahood itself. This is confirmed by the distinction between two aspects: the non-dual wisdom, which is essentially devoid of inherent existence <note>Sanskrit: niḥsvabhāva</note>, for it is certain that there is no duality. The aspects of duality set and vanish, while only the limitless [reality] appears as luminosity.

Those who possess great compassion are liberated by the six <term>pāramitās</term> <gloss>perfections</gloss> themselves; they are referred to as "great compassion" precisely for this reason. A <term>bodhisattva</term> <gloss>awakening being</gloss> who possesses great compassion works for the supreme benefit of sentient beings and aspires toward unsurpassed enlightenment, not toward the lesser path. This is achieved through the six perfections, not by one alone. If one were liberated by the six themselves, what then would be the role of the five, and what would the sixth accomplish?

Regarding the question "What are the fourfold purifications?", they are as follows:

For all sentient beings, all negative tendencies <term>dausthulya</term> <gloss>propensities for negative states or incapacity</gloss> of defilements have become entirely separated from their basis. Furthermore, one may take on a body as one wishes, and one has mastery over abiding and transmigrating. This is the purification of the basis.

Having mastery over emanations, matters pertaining to transformations, and all objects of focus is the purification of the object.

Since the mind is free from all negative tendencies, virtue increases in the mind in every respect; this is the purification of the mind.

Since one is free from all negative tendencies associated with ignorance, one's knowledge of all that is to be known is unobstructed and under one's command; this is the purification of primordial wisdom.

Regarding the question "What are the ten powers?", they are as follows:

To remain for as long as one wishes is the mastery of life.

To remain in states of meditative concentration, immeasurable states, and liberations—whichever state one wishes to abide in—according to one's desire, is the mastery of mind.

By saying that one correctly knows all phenomena as they truly are in the <term>dharmadhatu</term>, the text teaches that phenomena such as form are also correctly perceived merely as the <term>dharmadhatu</term>, and not otherwise. Because it is impossible to make sentient beings perceive them in a different way, they are designated as "signless" regarding form and the like, and the <term>dharmadhatu</term> itself is taught through skillful means. All of the Buddha’s teachings are also to be attained by the Bodhisattva, so it is said. When this was asked, the Blessed One did not approve of the phrasing "attaining the Buddha’s enlightenment." He then instructed, "Subhūti, what do you think? Is the Buddha’s enlightenment something that can be attained?" and so forth. He taught that because the Buddha and enlightenment are not separate, such language is untenable. Just as that phrasing is untenable, he showed that the statement "the Bodhisattva will attain enlightenment" is also untenable. Following this, while acknowledging that there is no difference between the Bodhisattva and enlightenment, he accepted that there is conventional terminology for the Bodhisattva attaining enlightenment. Then, by stating "Subhūti, in this regard, the great Bodhisattva fulfills the six perfections," and so forth, he taught the stages of attaining enlightenment. Therefore, he showed that enlightenment is attained by not abandoning the stages of what is conceptually imputed, rather than being attained instantaneously.

Following this, the purification of the Buddha-field was requested, and its distinctions are easy to understand. "Blessed One, should one call the great Bodhisattva 'determined' or 'undetermined'?" This is a question asking if the term Bodhisattva applies only to the determined state, or if it also applies to the undetermined state. "Or the aggregate of the Hearers, or the aggregate of the Solitary Realizers?" This is a question asking if the term Bodhisattva also applies to one who is determined as a Hearer or a Solitary Realizer. "Possessing such a body intentionally, and holding onto it through skillful means," means that because one has attained mastery over rebirth, one takes on rebirth, not involuntarily under the influence of karma. "Does the karma of the noble ones, which is free from outflows, lead to rebirth in the lower realms?" This refers to the eighth stage.

He overpowers the proponents of diverse views and the followers of other sects. He overpowers humanity with his splendor. Following this, he displays the miracle of magical transformation; specifically, he displays the miracle of emanated magical transformation. Regarding the phrase "in accordance with that, he reveals an ordinary body," this means that within a hundred billion universe systems, there is not a single sentient being, whether it be a Brahma, a god, a demon, or a human, before whom the Thus-Gone One does not appear, unless they lack the fortune <note>that is, the karmic ripeness</note> to perceive him. The phrase "in accordance with that" means that in order to put them at ease, he appears before each of them in a form matching the scale of their own bodies.

The phrase "ordinary body" means his natural body <note>referring to the Buddha's intrinsic or essential form</note>. What is this natural body like? It is a body of the Thus-Gone One that one can never tire of beholding. What is meant by a body one can never tire of beholding? It is a body whose complexion is unlike that of humans or gods, and for which there exists nothing in the world that can serve as a comparison; such is the complexion the natural body of the Thus-Gone One possesses. Although it appears to have a color, everyone recognizes it is not like the color of our own bodies. Likewise, while it possesses flesh, bones, hair, and nails, it is not like that of any other sentient being. Even though it appears in such a way, all worldly beings are struck with wonder. 

Thus, the body exists as the essence of a body; while it appears in that way and worldly beings are struck with wonder, no one can know what it truly is in its reality. In this way, although it resembles the bodies of all others in terms of shape, form, and so forth, its true nature remains unknown. A body that is extremely radiant and vast is called "that which one can never tire of beholding." It may be of the nature of <term>vajra</term> <gloss>diamond/adamantine</gloss>, or of the nature of gold, jewels, pearls, <term>vaidurya</term> <gloss>lapis lazuli</gloss>, and the like, or it may belong to the category of a human body, or to the body of a god or Brahma.
